problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（稀缺性、机会成本、显性成本与隐性成本、会计利润与经济利润）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

objective: Scarcity occurs when wants exceed the available supply of a resource.；Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone when making a choice.；Explicit costs are direct monetary payments; implicit costs are the value of resources used that are not paid for directly.

learningGoals.statement: Define scarcity and distinguish it from a temporary shortage.
Calculate opportunity cost correctly, excluding sunk costs.
Categorize costs as explicit or implicit in a given scenario.
Differentiate accounting profit from economic profit and explain why a business can have positive accounting profit but zero economic profit.
Interpret production possibilities curves, including constant vs. increasing marginal opportunity cost and factors that shift the PPC inward or outward.

knowledgeNodes.name: 稀缺性
knowledgeNodes.definition: A situation in which human wants for resources, goods, or services exceed the available supply, forcing choices.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.

knowledgeNodes.name: 机会成本
knowledgeNodes.definition: The value of the next best alternative that must be given up when making a choice.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.

knowledgeNodes.name: 显性成本与隐性成本
knowledgeNodes.definition: Explicit costs are direct monetary payments; implicit costs are the opportunity costs of using own resources (e.g., foregone rent or salary).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.

knowledgeNodes.name: 会计利润与经济利润
knowledgeNodes.definition: Accounting profit = total revenue minus explicit costs; economic profit = total revenue minus explicit and implicit costs.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Explain the main similarities and differences between various types of firms.

knowledgeNodes.name: 生产可能性曲线
knowledgeNodes.definition: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with available resources and technology, illustrating scarcity and opportunity cost.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of production possibilities curves and how they can be used to guide economic decisions about the allocation of scarce resources.

questions.successCriteria: Student selects the correct permanent nature of scarcity vs temporary shortage.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly addresses scarcity understanding required by B1.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can distinguish scarcity as a fundamental condition from a temporary shortage.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often think scarcity only happens during emergencies or when prices rise, confusing it with shortage.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes scarcity in economics?

options.label: A
options.text: A temporary situation where a product is unavailable due to supply chain disruption.
options.feedbackWrong: That describes a shortage, not scarcity. Scarcity is a permanent condition of unlimited wants vs limited resources.

options.label: B
options.text: A condition that exists when demand exceeds supply for a particular good at a specific time.
options.feedbackWrong: That's a shortage again. Scarcity is universal and ongoing.

options.label: C
options.text: The fundamental economic problem that wants exceed the available supply of resources at any time.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Scarcity is the basic condition that forces us to make choices.

options.label: D
options.text: Only occurs for natural resources like oil and diamonds.
options.feedbackWrong: Scarcity applies to all resources, not just natural ones. Time, labor, and capital are also scarce.

questions.successCriteria: Student correctly calculates opportunity cost excluding sunk costs.
questions.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
questions.alignmentNote: Specifically applies opportunity cost concept; officialNodeId not available for SE.
questions.stemIntent: See if student includes sunk costs in opportunity cost calculation.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often include past payments (like tuition) in opportunity cost even though they are sunk and not affected by the current decision.
questions.stem: A high school graduate is deciding whether to attend university or take a job paying $16,000 per year. University tuition is $20,000 per year, and books cost $2,000. What is the opportunity cost of attending university for one year?

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: This only includes explicit costs and ignores the foregone salary. Also, it includes all costs without considering what is truly given up.

options.label: B
options.text: $16,000 (foregone salary) + $20,000 (tuition) + $2,000 (books) = $38,000
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Opportunity cost includes both explicit costs (tuition+books) and implicit costs (foregone salary).

options.label: C
options.text: $16,000 (foregone salary) only
options.feedbackWrong: This ignores explicit costs. The tuition and books are also part of the cost of attending university.

options.label: D
options.text: $16,000 + $20,000 + $2,000 + any other costs already incurred, like application fees paid last month
options.feedbackWrong: Application fees are sunk costs and should not be included in opportunity cost of the current decision.

questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies implicit costs in a scenario.
questions.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
questions.alignmentNote: Implicit costs are a component of opportunity cost.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can distinguish explicit from implicit costs.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think only monetary payments count as costs; they often miss foregone salary or rent as implicit costs.
questions.stem: A McDonald's manager earning $12,000 per year quits to open her own restaurant. She uses her own savings (which were earning $1,000 interest per year) and her own building (which she could rent out for $24,000 per year). In her first year, total revenue is $80,000 and explicit expenses (wages, supplies, etc.) are $50,000. Which of the following is an implicit cost for her restaurant?

options.label: A
options.text: Wages paid to employees: $30,000
options.feedbackWrong: That is an explicit cost – a direct monetary payment.

options.label: B
options.text: Foregone salary as manager: $12,000
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Foregone salary is an implicit cost because it is a non‑monetary opportunity cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Cost of supplies: $20,000
options.feedbackWrong: Supplies are an explicit cost – you pay for them directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Rent paid to landlord: $24,000
options.feedbackWrong: If she pays rent to a landlord, that is explicit. But if she uses her own building, the foregone rent is implicit. The question says she uses her own building, so the $24,000 is implicit, but careful: the option says "Rent paid" – that would be explicit. The correct implicit cost is the foregone rent, but here we need an implicit cost from the list. Note: The options mix explicit and implicit; the foregone salary is an implicit cost.

questions.successCriteria: Student recognizes that accounting profit ignores implicit costs and therefore can be positive even when economic profit is zero.
questions.ossdExpectation: Explain the main similarities and differences between various types of firms.
questions.alignmentNote: Accounting vs economic profit is central to understanding firm performance.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands that accounting profit does not account for opportunity costs and thus can overstate business success.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think a positive accounting profit automatically means the business is doing well, ignoring implicit costs.
questions.stem: Refer to the McDonald's manager scenario. Her accounting profit is $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000. But economic profit is zero. Why does the business still make sense from an accounting perspective but not from an economic perspective?

options.label: A
options.text: Accounting profit ignores implicit costs like the foregone manager salary and foregone interest/rent, so it overstates true profitability.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Economic profit subtracts implicit costs; when they equal the accounting profit, economic profit is zero.

options.label: B
options.text: Accounting profit includes more revenue than economic profit.
options.feedbackWrong: Revenue is the same; the difference is only in costs considered.

options.label: C
options.text: Economic profit is always lower than accounting profit, but that doesn't matter because owners care about cash flow.
options.feedbackWrong: Economic profit matters for long-term decision making. Positive accounting profit with negative economic profit may indicate the resources could be better used elsewhere.

options.label: D
options.text: Accounting profit is the same as economic profit when there are no explicit costs.
options.feedbackWrong: Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs. If there are implicit costs, they differ.

questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that a concave PPC represents increasing marginal opportunity cost.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of production possibilities curves and how they can be used to guide economic decisions about the allocation of scarce resources.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands the shape of PPC reflects opportunity cost behavior.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think all PPCs are straight lines or that concavity indicates constant opportunity cost.
questions.stem: A production possibilities curve that is concave (bowed outward) from the origin indicates:

options.label: A
options.text: Constant marginal opportunity cost.
options.feedbackWrong: A straight line indicates constant opportunity cost; a concave curve indicates increasing opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing marginal opportunity cost.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. As more of one good is produced, the opportunity cost in terms of the other good increases.

options.label: C
options.text: Decreasing marginal opportunity cost.
options.feedbackWrong: Decreasing opportunity cost would make the curve convex, not concave.

options.label: D
options.text: That resources are perfectly adaptable to producing either good.
options.feedbackWrong: Perfect adaptability would produce a straight line (constant opportunity cost). A concave curve implies resources are not equally well suited to both goods.

questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies which event shifts the PPC outward.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of production possibilities curves and how they can be used to guide economic decisions about the allocation of scarce resources.
questions.alignmentNote: Understanding shifts is part of PPC analysis.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows the direction of PPC shift for common economic events.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often think technological advancement shifts the PPC inward, or that a natural disaster shifts it outward.
questions.stem: Which of the following events would cause a country's production possibilities curve to shift outward (to the right)?

options.label: A
options.text: A major earthquake destroys factories and infrastructure.
options.feedbackWrong: A disaster reduces resources and shifts the PPC inward.

options.label: B
options.text: Adoption of new technology that increases productivity in all industries.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Technological advancement allows more output with same resources, shifting the PPC outward.

options.label: C
options.text: The government imposes stricter environmental regulations that reduce output.
options.feedbackWrong: Stricter regulations may reduce production possibilities, shifting the PPC inward.

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the labor force due to an aging population.
options.feedbackWrong: Fewer workers mean less production capacity, shifting the PPC inward.

questions.successCriteria: Student explains why sunk costs are irrelevant for future decisions and gives a correct example.
questions.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
questions.alignmentNote: Challenges deeper understanding of opportunity cost by excluding sunk costs.
questions.stemIntent: Assess if student can justify excluding sunk costs from opportunity cost calculations.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think money already spent should be considered in future choices.
questions.stem: Explain why sunk costs should not be included when calculating opportunity cost. Provide a brief example of a sunk cost from the lesson (e.g., application fees paid before deciding on university).
questions.rubric: Full marks: Clear explanation that sunk costs are already incurred and cannot be recovered, so they do not affect future choices; provides a relevant example (e.g., application fees). Partial: mentions sunk costs but lacks clarity or example. No marks: includes sunk costs in opportunity cost.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: Sunk costs are expenses that have already been paid and cannot be recovered. They should not be included in opportunity cost because opportunity cost only looks at future alternatives given up. For example, if a student paid $100 in university application fees last month, that money is gone regardless of the decision to attend or work. The opportunity cost of attending university should only include the tuition, books, and foregone salary, not the sunk application fees.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks answer that equates scarcity with a temporary shortage.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Thinks scarcity is a temporary condition that only arises when supplies run low, rather than a permanent condition of limited resources.

miniLesson.explain: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem that human wants for goods and services exceed the available supply of resources. It is a permanent condition that exists at all times, regardless of price or availability. In contrast, a shortage is a temporary situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price, often due to disruptions or hoarding. For example, during the pandemic, masks were in short supply, but the underlying resource (labor to produce masks) is not permanently scarce in the same sense as oil or time. Scarcity forces choices; shortage can be resolved by price adjustments or production increases.
miniLesson.example: Gold is scarce because there is a limited quantity on Earth. Even if no gold is being sold at a given moment, it remains scarce. By contrast, a shortage of gold jewelry during a holiday rush is temporary and can be alleviated by increasing supply or raising prices.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Scarcity is permanent like gravity; shortage is temporary like a rainstorm.

guidedPractice.prompt: Classify each situation as scarcity or shortage: a) There is a limited amount of fresh water on Earth. b) Due to a snowstorm, grocery stores run out of bread.
guidedPractice.answer: a) Scarcity (fresh water is limited overall). b) Shortage (temporary due to storm).

guidedPractice.prompt: During the pandemic, mask demand exceeded supply, causing prices to rise. Is this scarcity or shortage? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: This is a shortage. Masks are not permanently scarce; the condition was temporary due to sudden demand and supply chain issues. Scarcity would apply if we lacked the resources to produce any masks at all.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student argues: 'Since diamond producers hoard diamonds to keep prices high, diamonds are not truly scarce; they only appear scarce.' Evaluate this statement using the concepts of scarcity and shortage.
guidedPractice.answer: The student confuses scarcity with artificial shortage. Diamonds are naturally scarce because there is a finite quantity. Hoarding creates a temporary shortage by restricting supply, but scarcity exists regardless. Scarcity is the underlying condition; shortage is a market phenomenon. Even if hoarding stopped, diamonds would still be scarce.

reteachModules.trigger: Student includes sunk costs in opportunity cost calculations, as shown by selecting option D in diagnostic question 2 or giving a similar response.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Sunk costs, which are already incurred and cannot be recovered, are mistakenly included in the opportunity cost calculation.

miniLesson.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone when making a choice. It only includes future costs and benefits, not past expenses that cannot be changed. Sunk costs are irrelevant to current decisions.
miniLesson.example: A student deciding between college and work: opportunity cost includes foregone salary and current tuition, but not application fees already paid.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Sunk costs are like spilled milk – don't count them when deciding what to do next.

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify which of the following is a sunk cost and which is an opportunity cost: a $12 concert ticket bought last month, and $80 you could earn by working tonight.
guidedPractice.answer: Sunk cost: $12 ticket. Opportunity cost: $80 foregone earnings.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student bought a $12 concert ticket last month. If she attends the concert, she cannot work a shift that pays $80. What is the opportunity cost of attending the concert? Do not include the ticket cost.
guidedPractice.answer: $80. The $12 ticket is a sunk cost.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why the $12 ticket should not be included in the opportunity cost calculation from the previous question.
guidedPractice.answer: Because the $12 is already spent and cannot be recovered; it is a sunk cost. Opportunity cost only considers the value of the next best alternative that is given up by the current decision, which is the $80 wage.

reteachModules.trigger: When a student identifies a non-monetary opportunity cost as an explicit cost, or vice versa, such as treating foregone salary as an explicit cost.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often believe that only direct monetary payments count as costs, failing to recognize the value of resources they own (e.g., their own time or property) as implicit costs.

miniLesson.explain: In economics, costs are divided into explicit and implicit costs. Explicit costs are direct, out-of-pocket monetary payments made to others (e.g., wages, rent, supplies). Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of using resources that you already own; they represent forgone income or benefits from the next best alternative use of those resources. For example, if you quit a job to start a business, your foregone salary is an implicit cost. Understanding both types is essential for calculating economic profit.
miniLesson.example: Consider a manager who leaves a job paying $16,000 per year to open her own restaurant. She uses her own building (which could rent for $24,000 per year) and her own savings (which could earn $20,000 in interest). Her restaurant has total revenue of $80,000 and explicit costs of $20,000 (supplies, wages). The implicit costs are: foregone salary ($16,000), foregone rent ($24,000), and foregone interest ($20,000). Total implicit = $60,000. Accounting profit = $80,000 - $20,000 = $60,000. Economic profit = $80,000 - $20,000 - $60,000 = $0. This shows that even though accounting profit is positive, economic profit is zero because all resources are earning exactly their opportunity cost.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Explicit = Money leaving your pocket. Implicit = Money you could have earned but didn't.

guidedPractice.prompt: In the scenario above, which of the following is an implicit cost? A) Wages paid to employees ($20,000). B) Foregone salary ($16,000). C) Cost of supplies. D) Rent paid to landlord (if any).
guidedPractice.answer: B) Foregone salary ($16,000). The foregone salary is an implicit cost because it is the value of the next best alternative given up, not a direct monetary payment.

guidedPractice.prompt: Categorize each cost as explicit (E) or implicit (I): a) $20,000 spent on restaurant supplies. b) $24,000 rent that could have been earned from the building. c) $16,000 salary given up from previous job. d) $80,000 in total revenue.
guidedPractice.answer: a) E (supplies are a direct payment). b) I (foregone rent is an opportunity cost of using own building). c) I (foregone salary is opportunity cost of own labor). d) Revenue is not a cost.

guidedPractice.prompt: Using the same scenario, calculate the economic profit if the explicit costs were $20,000, total revenue $80,000, and implicit costs were $60,000. Explain why the owner might still be satisfied even though economic profit is zero.
guidedPractice.answer: Economic profit = $80,000 - $20,000 - $60,000 = $0. The owner might be satisfied because the accounting profit ($60,000) is positive, but economically, she is earning exactly what she could earn elsewhere. A zero economic profit means she is covering all her opportunity costs, so there is no better alternative available.

reteachModules.trigger: Student believes that a positive accounting profit always indicates a successful business, ignoring implicit costs.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think accounting profit is the complete measure of profitability and overlook the opportunity costs of using own resources.

miniLesson.explain: Accounting profit = total revenue − explicit costs. Economic profit = total revenue − explicit costs − implicit costs (opportunity costs). A business can have positive accounting profit but zero or negative economic profit if implicit costs are high. Economic profit tells whether the firm is truly earning more than the next best alternative.
miniLesson.example: Consider a manager who leaves a $12,000 salary to open a restaurant. She uses her own building (foregone rent $24,000). Annual revenue $80,000, explicit costs (wages, supplies) $44,000. Accounting profit = $80,000 − $44,000 = $36,000. But implicit costs = $12,000 (salary) + $24,000 (rent) = $36,000. Economic profit = $80,000 − $44,000 − $36,000 = $0. The business earns exactly what she gave up, so it is not a superior use of resources.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Accounting profit is like a gross measure; economic profit is net of everything given up. Always ask: 'What am I giving up that I don't pay for?' to find implicit costs.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does accounting profit ignore that economic profit includes?
guidedPractice.answer: Accounting profit ignores implicit costs (opportunity costs of using own resources). Economic profit includes both explicit and implicit costs.

guidedPractice.prompt: A baker gives up a job paying $20,000 per year and uses her own shop (foregone rent $24,000). Total revenue is $80,000 and explicit costs are $20,000. Calculate accounting profit and economic profit.

A freelancer leaves a $12,000 salary, uses her own equipment (foregone rent $4,000). Revenue $80,000, explicit costs $12,000. Accounting profit is $68,000. Is this business a better use of resources than her next best alternative? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: Economic profit = $80,000 − $12,000 − ($12,000 + $4,000) = $52,000. Since economic profit is positive ($52,000), the business is a better use of resources than the next best alternative.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an answer indicating all PPCs are straight lines or does not recognize concave PPC as representing increasing opportunity cost.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students believe that the production possibilities curve is always a straight line, and they do not understand that a concave (bowed-outward) shape reflects increasing marginal opportunity cost as more of one good is produced.

miniLesson.explain: The production possibilities curve (PPC) shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce. Its shape reveals how opportunity cost behaves. A straight-line PPC means constant marginal opportunity cost: each additional unit of one good always costs the same amount of the other good. A concave (bowed-outward) PPC means increasing marginal opportunity cost: as you produce more of one good, you must give up increasing amounts of the other good. This typically occurs because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods—first you use the most efficient resources, then less efficient ones, raising the opportunity cost.
miniLesson.example: Consider an economy that can produce either robots or wheat. With a straight-line PPC, producing every 10 robots costs exactly 20 tons of wheat. With a concave PPC, producing the first 10 robots costs 20 tons of wheat, but producing the next 10 robots costs 24 tons of wheat because the best wheat land must be converted, giving up more wheat per robot.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Straight PPC = same sacrifice each time (constant cost). Curved PPC = each extra unit costs more (increasing cost).

guidedPractice.prompt: A production possibilities curve is a straight line. What does this indicate about marginal opportunity cost?

On a concave PPC, producing the first 12 units of good A requires giving up 20 units of good B. Producing the next 12 units of good A requires giving up 24 units of good B. Is opportunity cost constant or increasing?
Explain why a PPC might be concave (bowed outward) rather than a straight line. Use a real-world example involving a factory that can produce widgets and gadgets.
guidedPractice.answer: Because resources are not equally efficient in producing both goods. For example, a factory can produce widgets and gadgets. The first workers switched to gadgets are the best gadget makers, so few widgets are lost. As more workers are switched, they are less skilled at gadgets, so more widgets are given up per gadget. This increasing opportunity cost makes the PPC concave.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an event that shifts the PPC in the wrong direction (e.g., chooses a disaster as outward shift).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses which events increase or decrease an economy's production capacity, leading to incorrect inward/outward PPC shifts.

miniLesson.explain: The production possibilities curve (PPC) shifts outward (to the right) when the economy's productive capacity increases due to factors like technological advancements, increases in natural resources, or beneficial government policies. It shifts inward (to the left) when capacity decreases due to disasters, resource depletion, or harmful policies. The key is whether the event expands or contracts the total amount of goods/services that can be produced.
miniLesson.example: A new farming technology that increases crop yields per hectare allows the economy to produce more food and other goods with the same resources, shifting the PPC outward. Conversely, a drought that destroys farmland reduces output capacity, shifting the PPC inward.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Outward = Opportunity for more; Inward = In trouble. Think of the PPC as a balloon: adding air (improvements) expands it out; letting air out (losses) shrinks it in.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of these events would cause a country's production possibilities curve to shift outward? A) A new computer system increases factory efficiency. B) A hurricane destroys key infrastructure.
guidedPractice.answer: A) A new computer system increases factory efficiency.

guidedPractice.prompt: A country discovers new oil reserves. Does this shift the PPC inward or outward? Explain briefly.
guidedPractice.answer: Outward. The discovery increases the available natural resources, allowing the economy to produce more goods (e.g., energy and products derived from oil) with the same other resources, thus expanding production capacity.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose a government imposes strict pollution controls that reduce factory output by 20% across all industries. Does the PPC shift? If so, which direction? Explain your reasoning using the concept of opportunity cost.
guidedPractice.answer: Yes, the PPC shifts inward. The regulations reduce the maximum amount of goods the economy can produce, decreasing productive capacity. This means the economy must give up more of one good to produce a given amount of another, reflecting a higher opportunity cost due to the constraint.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios represents scarcity rather than a temporary shortage?
options: A high demand for concert tickets leads to sold-out shows within minutes.
The global supply of rare earth metals is limited due to geological factors.
A factory shutdown causes a temporary lack of car parts.
Holiday shopping causes popular toys to sell out.

questions.stem: A student says: 'Scarcity doesn't exist because whenever there is a shortage, producers can always increase supply and prices will adjust.' Critically evaluate this statement using the concepts of scarcity and shortage.
questions.rubric: Must explain that scarcity is a permanent condition of limited resources, while shortage is a temporary market imbalance. Should note that increasing supply cannot eliminate scarcity (e.g., land, time). Award 1 point for correct definition of scarcity, 1 for correct definition of shortage, 1 for explaining why the student's argument is flawed. Score at least 2 out of 3 to pass.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly. For open-ended, score at least 2 out of 3 points.

questions.stem: A student bought a $12 concert ticket last month. She now has the opportunity to work a shift that pays $80. If she attends the concert, what is the opportunity cost?
Explain why the $12 ticket is not part of the opportunity cost of attending the concert.
questions.rubric: Student must state that the $12 ticket is a sunk cost (already spent and cannot be recovered) and that opportunity cost only includes the value of the next best alternative foregone (the $80 wage). A clear explanation with both points is required.

retestCards.passRule: Must answer multiple-choice correctly and provide a satisfactory explanation in open-ended.

questions.stem: A freelance graphic designer quits a full-time job to start his own studio. Which of the following is an implicit cost?
options: Cost of a new computer
Rent for studio space
Foregone salary from the full-time job
Payment to a part-time assistant

questions.stem: A freelance writer leaves a job paying $16,000 per year to start a blog. She uses her home office (foregone rent of $24,000 per year) and $20,000 of savings that could have earned $2,000 in interest. In her first year, she earns $144,000 in total revenue. Her explicit costs are $80,000 for supplies, software, and marketing. Calculate the accounting profit and the economic profit. Explain whether she should continue in the long run.
questions.rubric: Correctly calculates accounting profit ($64,000). Correctly identifies implicit costs: foregone salary ($16,000), foregone rent ($24,000), foregone interest ($2,000) totaling $42,000. Correctly calculates economic profit ($22,000). Explains that positive economic profit means she is covering all opportunity costs and should continue.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select correct option in Q1 and answer Q2 correctly: list all three implicit costs (foregone salary, foregone rent, foregone interest) and compute accounting profit = $64,000 and economic profit = $22,000.

questions.stem: A software developer leaves a job paying $12,000 per year to start her own app company. She uses her own apartment as an office, giving up $24,000 in annual rent. Her revenue is $80,000 and explicit costs are $20,000. Which of the following is true?
options: Accounting profit is $60,000 and economic profit is $60,000.
Accounting profit is $60,000 and economic profit is $24,000.
Accounting profit is $60,000 and economic profit is $0.
Accounting profit is $60,000 and economic profit is -$36,000.

questions.stem: Explain why a business with positive accounting profit might still be considered unsuccessful by an economist. Use an example that includes at least one implicit cost.
questions.rubric: Response must include: (1) definition of economic profit including implicit costs, (2) example showing accounting profit positive but economic profit lower or negative, (3) explanation that positive economic profit indicates better use of resources.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer the multiple-choice question correctly and provide an explanation that references implicit costs and economic profit in the open-ended question.

questions.stem: A production possibilities curve that is a straight line indicates:
options: Constant marginal opportunity cost
Increasing marginal opportunity cost
Decreasing marginal opportunity cost
No opportunity cost

questions.stem: Explain why a production possibilities curve is often concave (bowed outward) rather than a straight line. Use a specific example involving two goods of your choice to illustrate increasing marginal opportunity cost.
questions.rubric: Student must state that concave PPC reflects increasing marginal opportunity cost because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods. Example must show that as more of one good is produced, the opportunity cost (amount of the other good given up) increases. Full credit for clear explanation with concrete numbers or scenario.

questions.stem: Which of the following events would cause a country's production possibilities curve to shift outward?
options: A severe earthquake destroys factories and infrastructure.
A new technology improves manufacturing efficiency across all industries.
A prolonged labor strike reduces the available workforce.
Depletion of essential natural resources like coal and oil.

questions.stem: Explain why a pandemic that significantly reduces the size of the labor force would shift a nation's production possibilities curve inward. Use the concept of productive capacity in your answer.
questions.rubric: The student must state that the pandemic reduces the available labor resource, which decreases the economy's maximum output of all goods. This shrinks productive capacity, causing the PPC to shift inward (left). Partial credit for mentioning reduction in resources or capacity.

learningGoals.statement: Define scarcity and distinguish it from a temporary shortage.
Calculate opportunity cost correctly, excluding sunk costs.
Categorize costs as explicit or implicit in a given scenario.
Differentiate accounting profit from economic profit and explain why a business can have positive accounting profit but zero economic profit.
Interpret production possibilities curves, including constant vs. increasing marginal opportunity cost and factors that shift the PPC inward or outward.

nextActions: [err-scarcity-vs-shortage] student picks an answer that equates scarcity with a temporary shortage: Scarcity is a permanent condition of limited resources, not a temporary shortage. Let's review the difference.

[err-opportunity-cost-including-sunk-cost] student includes past, irrecoverable costs in opportunity cost calculation: Opportunity cost only includes the value of the next best alternative foregone, not costs already incurred. Let's practice.

[err-explicit-implicit-confusion] student misidentifies an explicit cost as implicit or vice versa: Explicit costs are direct monetary payments; implicit costs are non‑monetary opportunity costs. Let's clarify.

[err-accounting-profit-as-true-profit] student thinks accounting profit alone indicates business success without considering implicit costs: Accounting profit ignores implicit costs. Economic profit gives a fuller picture. Let's revisit the concept.

[err-ppc-constant-vs-increasing] student assumes all PPCs are straight lines and does not recognize increasing opportunity cost: PPCs can be straight (constant opportunity cost) or concave (increasing opportunity cost). Let's explore both.

[err-ppc-shift-direction] student confuses which events shift the PPC inward vs outward: Remember: improvements in technology or resource availability shift the PPC outward; disasters or resource depletion shift it inward.

cards.question: Which statement best describes scarcity in economics?
options: A temporary situation where a product is unavailable due to supply chain disruption.
A condition that exists when demand exceeds supply for a particular good at a specific time.
The fundamental economic problem that wants exceed the available supply of resources at any time.
Only occurs for natural resources like oil and diamonds.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can distinguish scarcity as a fundamental condition from a temporary shortage.
misconceptions: That describes a shortage, not scarcity. Scarcity is a permanent condition of unlimited wants vs limited resources.
That's a shortage again. Scarcity is universal and ongoing.
✓ Correct. Scarcity is the basic condition that forces us to make choices.
Scarcity applies to all resources, not just natural ones. Time, labor, and capital are also scarce.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects the correct permanent nature of scarcity vs temporary shortage.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly addresses scarcity understanding required by B1.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often think scarcity only happens during emergencies or when prices rise, confusing it with shortage.

cards.question: A high school graduate is deciding whether to attend university or take a job paying $16,000 per year. University tuition is $20,000 per year, and books cost $2,000. What is the opportunity cost of attending university for one year?
options: $16,000 (foregone salary) + $20,000 (tuition) + $2,000 (books) = $38,000
$16,000 (foregone salary) only
$16,000 + $20,000 + $2,000 + any other costs already incurred, like application fees paid last month
cards.diagnosis: See if student includes sunk costs in opportunity cost calculation.
misconceptions: This only includes explicit costs and ignores the foregone salary. Also, it includes all costs without considering what is truly given up.
✓ Correct. Opportunity cost includes both explicit costs (tuition+books) and implicit costs (foregone salary).
This ignores explicit costs. The tuition and books are also part of the cost of attending university.
Application fees are sunk costs and should not be included in opportunity cost of the current decision.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly calculates opportunity cost excluding sunk costs.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.alignmentNote: Specifically applies opportunity cost concept; officialNodeId not available for SE.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often include past payments (like tuition) in opportunity cost even though they are sunk and not affected by the current decision.

cards.question: A McDonald's manager earning $12,000 per year quits to open her own restaurant. She uses her own savings (which were earning $1,000 interest per year) and her own building (which she could rent out for $24,000 per year). In her first year, total revenue is $80,000 and explicit expenses (wages, supplies, etc.) are $50,000. Which of the following is an implicit cost for her restaurant?
options: Wages paid to employees: $30,000
Foregone salary as manager: $12,000
Cost of supplies: $20,000
Rent paid to landlord: $24,000
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can distinguish explicit from implicit costs.
misconceptions: That is an explicit cost – a direct monetary payment.
✓ Correct. Foregone salary is an implicit cost because it is a non‑monetary opportunity cost.
Supplies are an explicit cost – you pay for them directly.

If she pays rent to a landlord, that is explicit. But if she uses her own building, the foregone rent is implicit. The question says she uses her own building, so the $24,000 is implicit, but careful: the option says "Rent paid" – that would be explicit. The correct implicit cost is the foregone rent, but here we need an implicit cost from the list. Note: The options mix explicit and implicit; the foregone salary is an implicit cost.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies implicit costs in a scenario.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.alignmentNote: Implicit costs are a component of opportunity cost.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think only monetary payments count as costs; they often miss foregone salary or rent as implicit costs.

cards.question: Refer to the McDonald's manager scenario. Her accounting profit is $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000. But economic profit is zero. Why does the business still make sense from an accounting perspective but not from an economic perspective?
options: Accounting profit ignores implicit costs like the foregone manager salary and foregone interest/rent, so it overstates true profitability.
Accounting profit includes more revenue than economic profit.
Economic profit is always lower than accounting profit, but that doesn't matter because owners care about cash flow.
Accounting profit is the same as economic profit when there are no explicit costs.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that accounting profit does not account for opportunity costs and thus can overstate business success.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. Economic profit subtracts implicit costs; when they equal the accounting profit, economic profit is zero.
Revenue is the same; the difference is only in costs considered.
Economic profit matters for long-term decision making. Positive accounting profit with negative economic profit may indicate the resources could be better used elsewhere.
Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs. If there are implicit costs, they differ.
cards.successCriteria: Student recognizes that accounting profit ignores implicit costs and therefore can be positive even when economic profit is zero.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain the main similarities and differences between various types of firms.
cards.alignmentNote: Accounting vs economic profit is central to understanding firm performance.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think a positive accounting profit automatically means the business is doing well, ignoring implicit costs.

cards.question: A production possibilities curve that is concave (bowed outward) from the origin indicates:
options: Constant marginal opportunity cost.
Increasing marginal opportunity cost.
Decreasing marginal opportunity cost.
That resources are perfectly adaptable to producing either good.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands the shape of PPC reflects opportunity cost behavior.
misconceptions: A straight line indicates constant opportunity cost; a concave curve indicates increasing opportunity cost.
✓ Correct. As more of one good is produced, the opportunity cost in terms of the other good increases.
Decreasing opportunity cost would make the curve convex, not concave.
Perfect adaptability would produce a straight line (constant opportunity cost). A concave curve implies resources are not equally well suited to both goods.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that a concave PPC represents increasing marginal opportunity cost.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of production possibilities curves and how they can be used to guide economic decisions about the allocation of scarce resources.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think all PPCs are straight lines or that concavity indicates constant opportunity cost.

cards.question: Which of the following events would cause a country's production possibilities curve to shift outward (to the right)?
options: A major earthquake destroys factories and infrastructure.
Adoption of new technology that increases productivity in all industries.
The government imposes stricter environmental regulations that reduce output.
A decrease in the labor force due to an aging population.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the direction of PPC shift for common economic events.
misconceptions: A disaster reduces resources and shifts the PPC inward.
✓ Correct. Technological advancement allows more output with same resources, shifting the PPC outward.
Stricter regulations may reduce production possibilities, shifting the PPC inward.
Fewer workers mean less production capacity, shifting the PPC inward.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies which event shifts the PPC outward.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of production possibilities curves and how they can be used to guide economic decisions about the allocation of scarce resources.
cards.alignmentNote: Understanding shifts is part of PPC analysis.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often think technological advancement shifts the PPC inward, or that a natural disaster shifts it outward.

cards.question: Explain why sunk costs should not be included when calculating opportunity cost. Provide a brief example of a sunk cost from the lesson (e.g., application fees paid before deciding on university).
cards.diagnosis: Assess if student can justify excluding sunk costs from opportunity cost calculations.
cards.successCriteria: Student explains why sunk costs are irrelevant for future decisions and gives a correct example.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.alignmentNote: Challenges deeper understanding of opportunity cost by excluding sunk costs.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think money already spent should be considered in future choices.
